opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that Anthropic's whole approach, through the Responsible Scaling Policy, rests on making claims about our models: claims like "this model doesn't have dangerous capability X," or "if it did, these mitigations would be sufficient." My team's job is to stress test those claims. We try to find the places where the story we're telling ourselves about safety might be wrong, before reality finds them for us.

How that plays out changes a lot as you move up the AI safety levels. At the lower levels, the key safety arguments are mostly about capabilities. The model just can't do the dangerous thing, so the main question is whether our evaluations are actually measuring what we think. Are we eliciting the model's full capabilities, or could a bit more scaffolding or fine-tuning unlock something we missed? Stress testing there is largely red-teaming the evals themselves.

As you get to higher levels, you can no longer rely on "the model can't do it." You have to start relying on "the model won't do it," or "even if it tried, we'd catch it." That's a much harder kind of claim to make, and it's where things like alignment and the possibility of deception become central. If a model could be strategically hiding its capabilities or its goals, then a lot of standard evaluation methodology starts to break down. A big part of what we've tried to do, with work like model organisms of misalignment, the sleeper agents work, and the alignment faking work, is build concrete examples of those failure modes so we can test whether our safety techniques actually hold up against them. Does safety training remove a backdoor? Does a model that appears aligned stay aligned under different conditions? If our mitigations fail against a model we deliberately built to be problematic, that's a strong signal they might fail against one that got that way naturally.

So the purpose stays the same throughout: be the internal adversary to Anthropic's own safety case. But what the adversary is focused on shifts, from "are we measuring capabilities correctly?" toward "would our safety arguments survive a model that's actively working against them?" And ideally we're doing that work ahead of time, so when we hit those levels we already understand where the weak points are, rather than discovering them in deployment.

r002.rationale: It says stress testing checks whether safety techniques and mitigations hold up, but does not state that this is the aim of ASL-3 testing to prevent dangerous use.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the core of Anthropic's safety plan, as laid out in the Responsible Scaling Policy, is that as models get more capable, we make affirmative claims about them. We say "this model does not have dangerous capabilities past a certain threshold," or "our safeguards are sufficient to prevent this class of misuse," or, as we move further up the ASL ladder, "this model is not going to pursue goals that are at odds with what we want it to do in some coherent, sustained way." And the natural question is: how do you actually know that? It's very easy to write down a safety case. It's much harder to write down one that's actually true.

So the purpose of stress testing, as I see it, is to be the adversary to those claims. Our job is to go in and try to break them. If the alignment team says "we think this model is aligned because of X, Y, and Z," we want to go find the scenario where X, Y, and Z hold and the model still does something bad. If the safeguards team says "the classifier catches this category of misuse," we want to be the ones going in with the weird jailbreak or the unusual framing that gets around it. And a lot of my own work has been on the alignment side of that: things like the sleeper agents work, or alignment faking, where we're basically asking, can we construct a model that looks fine under all the evaluations we'd normally run and yet is actually pursuing something else? Because if we can construct that, then we know the evaluations alone aren't sufficient to support the claim.

And I think the reason that matters more as you go up through the safety levels is that the claims get more load-bearing and harder to verify. At ASL-2 or ASL-3, the claims are mostly about capability and misuse, and you can get a lot of mileage from pretty direct evaluations. You just test whether the model can do the thing. But once you're at the point where the concern is something like "this model might be capable enough to undermine our ability to oversee it," the claim you're making is about the model's dispositions, its goals, what it would do in situations you haven't tested. And that's exactly the regime where naive evaluation can fail, because a sufficiently capable model that had bad goals might also be capable of looking good on your evaluations. So you need some independent line of evidence that the thing you're measuring is what you think you're measuring, and that's where stress testing, model organisms, and interpretability all start to interlock.

I'd also say there's a kind of organizational function to it that I think is underrated. When you're a lab that's trying to ship models, there's always going to be some pressure for the people building the safety case to be optimistic about it. Not maliciously, just, you know, you built the thing, you want it to be fine. Having a group whose explicit remit is to be skeptical, to try to find the failure, and to be rewarded for finding it rather than for signing off, is a structural check on that. And ideally the output isn't just "we found a problem," it's "here's a concrete failure mode, here's a model organism that exhibits it, now go build the technique that actually catches it." So it's adversarial, but it's adversarial in a way that's meant to feed back into the rest of the safety work and make the eventual claims stronger, rather than just being a thumbs-up or thumbs-down at the end.

r002.rationale: It describes stress testing safeguards and trying to bypass them, but does not specifically state that the aim is to determine whether ASL-3 mitigations adequately prevent dangerous use.

r003.rationale: The response discusses concerns about alignment at higher safety levels, but does not say Anthropic does not yet know what would suffice to align models at ASL-4.

r004.rationale: It says stress testing can reveal failure modes and strengthen safety work, but does not connect that testing to providing evidence of danger if alignment at ASL-4 cannot be solved.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic purpose is to test whether the safeguards we’re relying on actually hold up as models become more capable. You don’t want to infer that a system is safe just because you haven’t observed it doing anything dangerous in ordinary use. You want to actively look for situations where your safety measures fail.

As you move through AI safety levels, the stakes and the relevant capabilities change, so the testing has to change too. At each stage, you need evidence that the protections are adequate for that level of risk. Stress testing is a way of finding gaps in that evidence before you rely on those protections in deployment. It doesn’t give you a proof of safety, but it can reveal reasons that your current safety case isn’t good enough.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the purpose is to understand whether the safeguards we’re relying on actually hold up as the models become more capable. As you move up through the AI safety levels, the risks you’re concerned about become more serious, and so the evidence you need becomes stronger.

You don’t just want to observe that a model behaves safely in ordinary use. You want to actively look for circumstances where it doesn’t—where somebody can get around a safeguard, or where an evaluation is missing an important capability. And then you want those findings to feed back into the deployment decision and the protections you put in place.

So I’d think of stress testing as a way of challenging the safety case. It’s not a proof that everything is safe. It’s a way to find weaknesses before you’re depending on those protections in a higher-stakes setting.
